h: Shakespeare, the Brontës and a rooftop view
p: The gallery reopened in 2023 after a major makeover, with a brand-new entrance on its north side, brighter rooms and a fresh hang that brings far more women and people from different backgrounds into the story. If you last visited years ago, it's well worth another look, because it genuinely feels like a different place.

A few portraits are worth seeking out. The Chandos portrait, thought to show William Shakespeare, was the very first work to join the collection, and it's one of the few images with a real claim to being painted from life. The Brontë sisters' portrait, painted by their brother Branwell, has a ghostly gap in the middle where he painted himself out, and you can still make out his shadowy shape. Then there are the grand Tudor pictures of Elizabeth I, which are basically royal PR in paint.

The Tudor rooms at the top are a good place to begin, as the collection broadly runs from the oldest at the top down to the present day lower down. Work your way through the centuries and you'll see how the idea of who deserves a portrait keeps changing, from monarchs and courtiers to campaigners, musicians and sporting heroes.

An hour and a half to two hours is plenty for a good look. The rooftop restaurant has a cracking view over Trafalgar Square towards Whitehall and the Houses of Parliament, so it's worth a peek even if you're only stopping for a drink. Once you're back outside, Chinatown is a few minutes north for a cheap and cheerful lunch, and St Martin-in-the-Fields sits right across the road.
